title: Why Test Preparation Isn't a One-Exam Business Anymore
deck: PTE Academic volume is up 90% in a year, and the SAT just completed its shift to fully digital testing. Neither trend points to a single default exam.
imageAlt: Student filling in an answer sheet during an exam
body: For years, the standardized test that mattered for study abroad was the one your target country's institutions asked for, and that was usually IELTS. That's no longer the whole picture. Pearson's PTE Academic saw global volumes rise 90% in a single year (2022 vs. 2021), a scale of growth that reflects more institutions and immigration authorities accepting a computer-delivered format, not just more people testing. Meanwhile, admissions testing has been going through its own transition: more than 1.97 million students in the US high school Class of 2024 took the SAT at least once, up from 1.91 million the year before, the same year the SAT Suite completed its full move to digital testing everywhere it's offered. Colleges that had gone test-optional during the pandemic have also been reinstating score requirements, citing the SAT's value in identifying students likely to succeed. The practical result for anyone preparing for international study or migration: knowing one exam well is no longer enough. Effective preparation now means current, format-specific expertise across whichever combination of tests — IELTS, PTE, SAT, GRE, GMAT — a student's actual pathway requires, which is exactly the breadth Admizz Institute is built to cover.

title: What the Global Student Mobility Data Actually Shows
deck: International students contributed $42.9 billion to the US economy alone in 2024/25, inside a global market projected to more than double by 2030.
imageAlt: Diverse group of university students in a lecture hall
body: International student mobility is easy to describe in the abstract — a growing number of people choosing to study outside their home country — and much more interesting once you look at the actual scale involved. In the US alone, 1.18 million international students enrolled in 2024/25, up 5% on the year before. Behind that headline enrollment number is a real economic footprint: those students contributed $42.9 billion to the US economy in the same academic year, supporting more than 355,000 jobs in higher education, accommodation, retail, transportation and other sectors that a purely academic framing of 'international education' tends to leave out. Zoom out further and the trend holds: HolonIQ projects the global international-education market will more than double, from roughly $196 billion to $433 billion, by 2030. None of this happens evenly. Visa policy, post-study work rights and processing speed now shape where students actually go as much as program quality does — which is precisely why counseling built around more than one destination country, rather than a single default market, is the more resilient model. That breadth, across test prep, university partnerships and visa support, is what Admizz Education is structured to provide.

title: The Vocational Rehabilitation Employment Gap, By the Numbers
deck: 872,460 people received vocational rehabilitation services nationally in a single cohort — the real test of the system is how many of them end up with a job.
imageAlt: Colleagues in conversation at a modern workspace
body: Vocational rehabilitation is one of the largest, least-discussed workforce programs in the country. In the 2023/24 cohort, state VR programs reported serving 872,460 people nationally under the Workforce Innovation and Opportunity Act. Of those who exited the program in that period, 52.1% recorded a measurable skill gain — real evidence the training itself works. The harder number is what happens next: 55.9% of exiters had a job within two quarters of leaving the program. That's real progress, and it's also the actual size of the gap left to close. Context helps explain why that gap exists: nationally, the employment rate for people with a disability is 22.8%, against an 8.3% unemployment rate — roughly double the unemployment rate for people without a disability. Skills training that doesn't convert into employment isn't failing on its own terms; it's running into a labor market that hasn't caught up. Closing the distance between services received and jobs actually held — through hands-on training, employer partnerships and follow-through past the point of course completion — is the specific problem Admizz Workforce Solutions exists to work on.
